segments.text: The true answers about the assistant's decisions arrive hours or days later.
Measure quality anyway: decide which quick signals to watch until then,
and how many tickets people must check.
You feel ill, and the doctor takes a blood sample.
The lab result comes in three days, and it is the truth: it says what you have.
The doctor does not wait three days and do nothing.
A nurse checks your temperature and pulse every few hours.
These quick signs do not give the diagnosis.
But if your temperature jumps, the doctor acts at once, without the lab.
And the lab does not test all your blood.
A small sample is enough, if it is taken well.
A bigger one is surer, and costs more.
The assistant lives with the same three facts.
The truth comes late, the quick signs come early, and the truth comes from a sample.
Larkfield's quality goal is that ninety percent of reviewed tickets agree with the agent.
Priya wrote an alert: it fires when more than ten percent of the last thirty
minutes of reviews disagree.
In the drift run, agreement fell to eighty-five point three percent.
Almost fifteen percent disagreed.
The alert did not fire.
The run lasted under thirty minutes, so the window always held every review since the start.
The good old reviews hid the bad new ones: the highest disagreement it ever saw was
seven point nine percent.
And a second problem: when the quality falls, the reviews that would show it do not exist yet.
At Larkfield, they come hours or days later.
A label is the true answer for one input: the right team,
and whether a person had to handle the ticket.
At Larkfield, labels come from the agents' reviews.
A delayed label arrives long after the decision.
It is the lab result, and the quality and safety goals can only use these.
A proxy signal is a quick signal that often moves with quality, but is not quality.
It is the temperature: an answer without text, a jump in tokens,
or in the share sent to a person.
Proxies tell you where to look.
Put them on one timeline.
The ticket arrives, the triage is done three seconds later,
and the quick signals are known at once.
Then comes a gap: decisions made, not yet checked.
Only the review, hours or days later, closes it.
Agents reviewed twenty tickets, and seventeen agree: eighty-five percent.
Is the assistant below the ninety percent goal?
You cannot tell from twenty.
The Wilson interval gives the range of values that fit,
with ninety-five percent confidence: from sixty-four to almost ninety-five.
With a hundred reviews, the range still reaches above ninety.
Only with a thousand is the whole range below the goal.
Turn it around: how many reviews for a margin of five points near ninety percent?
A hundred and thirty-nine.
And a smaller margin costs much more, because the margin is squared.
Halve it, and you need four times the reviews.
Grace asks: how many tickets must my agents review?
Larkfield gets eight hundred and twenty-two tickets a day.
For a daily check, the agents review a hundred and thirty-nine: about one in six.
A weekly check needs the same number from a whole week, fewer than one in forty,
but you learn about a drop up to a week late.
Three rules.
Pick the tickets at random, not only the ones that customers complain about.
Sample by slice too: a hundred and thirty-nine random reviews hold only about seven
French tickets.
And safety is not a sample.
With a hundred and thirty-nine reviews and no miss,
the true miss rate could still be up to two point seven percent.
A sample cannot prove "none", so safety needs a rule on every ticket.
Which quick signal would have warned you before the reviews?
Compare two practice incidents.
Last week, with prompt v3, a proxy jumped at once: one answer in ten had no text.
An alert sees that in about a minute.
In the drift run's policy-silent block, no proxy moved.
The decisions were valid, and wrong.
Only the reviews showed the drop, from ninety-five to eighty-five percent.
So proxies catch failures that show in the output: no text, errors, slow answers, a cost jump.
Reviews catch decisions that look fine and are wrong.
You need both.
Sam asks: why not let the assistant check itself, or ask a second model?
Priya answers: a model judge is another assistant, with its own mistakes.
It can help sort tickets for review.
But the goal is about what our agents say is right, so the label must come from them.
Use delayed labels for every quality and safety number, and write the delay next to the goal.
Count windows in reviews, not in minutes.
And never report a proxy as quality.
The cost is agent time: a hundred and thirty-nine reviews a day is two to five hours of work.
And quality is always known late.
To recap.
Labels tell you whether decisions are right, but they arrive late, and they come from a sample.
Read every agreement with its interval: a hundred and thirty-nine reviews for a
margin of five points.
Watch proxies for failures that show in the output, and never report them as quality.
Now compute an interval yourself, in the box in this lesson.
